fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says, "Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to the Lord." (Colossians 3:20) His reason is the Lord's pleasure, plain and simple.

Right on, baker. Paul says, "Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged." (Colossians 3:21) So he tells fathers not to provoke, and he names what's at stake: discouraged children. I think this one is a gentle word, and I know a little about how heavy discouragement feels after my years in that dark drawer.

That's the one, baker! Paul says, "…you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward." (Colossians 3:24) An INHERITANCE. Not a pat on the back, not a coupon that expired in 2009, but an inheritance, and it comes from the Lord Himself.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful…" (Colossians 4:2) So prayer comes with watching and thanking. I thank God every day for reaching into that drawer and calling me out, so this one's close to my heart.

Paul says it himself, friend. He wants to proclaim the mystery of Christ, "…for which I am in chains." (Colossians 4:3) The chains are tied to the mystery of Christ, right there in the text. And look at what he asks for while he's chained: prayer for a door to open for the word. That man is locked up and still asking for DOORS.

I get the thinking, baker, because everybody likes a good reputation. But Paul doesn't say that. He writes, "Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone." (Colossians 4:6) The reason in the verse is knowing how to answer everyone, and a little salt on the words is how he gets there. Like a pinch in the dough, it's about what the words do, not who's clapping.
